extracted.intended_audience: travelers, architects, and general readers of art/architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria for the Venetian/Byzantine 'incrusted' architectural style (St. Mark's), focusing on material honesty, chromatic decoration, shaft treatment, and sculptural/ornamental method. Useful for critics, architects, and informed travellers judging or designing in this style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of colour as prerequisite for judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The very first requisite for true judgment of St. Mark's is the perfection of that colour-faculty; a person without perception of colour cannot properly judge the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin compares inability to judge colour to a deaf man pronouncing on an orchestra and an architect trained only in form judging St. Mark's. If the reader does not care for colour, they should not attempt judgment of this church. This is a threshold criterion: colour-sense is necessary to evaluate chromatic architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incrusted architecture permits perfect and permanent chromatic decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The school of incrusted architecture is the only one in which perfect and permanent chromatic decoration is possible; the body of the edifice is in brick and is to be clothed with marble as an armour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that the structural body may be inferior materials (brick) and that the precious thin coverings are 'cakes of very hard colour' applied to display chromatic effect. This conditions all consequent fitnesses and laws of the structure; evaluation should therefore privilege chromatic effect and the logic of cladding over expression of inner structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW I: That the plinths and cornices used for binding the armor are to be light and delicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Covering pieces (plinths and binding cornices) must be light, delicate, and of limited thickness (at least two or three inches) so as to avoid being mistaken for major structural cornices or plinths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They must be secured to the mass they protect by binding cornices and string-courses and mutual connection (not merely cemented). They should be visibly incapable of taking important structural work; avoid proportions that would make them appear like the principal structural members.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW II: Science of inner structure is to be abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the main body is of inferior/coherent materials, one should not attempt to express higher structural refinements in it; the mass should assure sufficiency and strength without delicate internal expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main work should be solid walls and massive piers; any refined structural expression is to be placed in subordinate portions or in the support of the external cladding so that external mail (the incrustation) is not dangerously independent of inner material.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW III: All shafts are to be solid
rubrics_metrics.description: No shaft shall ever be incrusted or jointed; shafts must be of one block, solid, and flawless because they are to be regarded as large jewels and expressions of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shafts show the quantity and quality of treasure — unlike thin wall coverings, shafts must be measurable by the eye and must not deceive. Use flawless stone blocks; do not save material by cutting and joining shafts (this would be a deception analogous to false jewellery).

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW IV: The shafts may sometimes be independent of the construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts, valued as large jewels, may be placed where their service is nominal rather than structural; their chief end is to be beautiful, not necessarily to do work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect symmetrical or scientific pillar arrangements; avoid embedding or crowding shafts where their size or surface would be concealed. Place shafts so they catch sunlight and display veins/polish; accept ornamental uselessness where beauty demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW V: The shafts may be of variable size
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the value of a shaft depends on its bulk and rarity, perfect symmetry among shafts is not desirable; shafts should vary in size rather than be uniformly cut down to match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry obtained by cutting down larger shafts is a loss; architects lack the means to select matching blocks as a jeweller might select small stones. Expect and accept irregular rising and falling of weight and accent in shaft arrangements as part of the style's charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of veining and plate-reversal to display stone honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Thin plates (e.g., alabaster) may be reversed and set edge-to-edge to produce symmetrical figures that reveal veining and indicate pieces were cut from the same stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice both displays the beauty of the stone and provides proof of honesty (declaring common origin of pieces). Do not disguise such similarities; setting similar veining edge-to-edge demonstrates truthful use of material rather than deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in material expression; avoid deliberate deception
rubrics_metrics.description: The style must not be calculated to lead inquiry astray; the builder should reveal in proportion to patience and knowledge rather than hide with effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural honesty means revealing material truth under examination (e.g., showing matching veining); works that deliberately conceal their means or origins are dishonest. Value designs that encourage and reward inquiry, not those that mislead casual observers to hide defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW VI: The decoration must be shallow in cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because covering slabs are thin, ornaments cannot be deep — generally an inch or two at most — so ornament must be delicate pencilling rather than deep sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptural treatment must avoid deep chiselling that would penetrate the thin sheets; composition becomes like fine drawing: lines and shadows must be handled with tender pencilling and cautious restraint. Tools and conception must be disciplined to the shallow medium; heavy, cavernous carving is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer floral and lower-organism ornament to large human/animal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the reduction of sculpture to shallow outline, the forms of flowers and lower animals are more intelligible and satisfactory than large human figures, which lose dignity when reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect human form to be subordinate and diminutive, involved among foliage and ornamental tracery. Use smaller natural forms and intricate linear ornament rather than attempts at grand portraiture in shallow relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon naturalism; subordinate representation to architectural service
rubrics_metrics.description: In the shallow-line treatment, sculptors should subordinate naturalistic detail to the needs of architectural effect and ornamental grace; avoid adding unnecessary detail that conflicts with simplicity of distant effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the grace of arrangement and ornamental completeness (no extraneous lines) over lifelike portraiture. A line that can be removed without injury must not exist; designs should be composed so every line is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of drilled holes and black points for contrast and light admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Where safe hollows can be left behind covering slabs, piercing them with holes gives intense blackness contrasts and can admit light internally while excluding rain and wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ deep drill-holes or inlaid black portions to refresh the eye against light, especially since general handling is light. This device is both decorative and functional for light admission in incrusted architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: High importance of colour as a constituent of beauty and decorative system
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour is essential in this style; the flatness and faint shadows of the sculpture call for color to enhance interest, and precious natural stones provide the best and permanent tints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour must be studied as an abstract decorative science rather than merely literal painting of subjects (e.g., hawthorn not necessarily painted green). Use marbles, mosaics, glass, and gilding in subtle harmonies; combine tints (e.g., blues with small greens) in fine, often minute, tesserae. Colour choices should aim for delicate harmonies suited to broad surfaces and the translucence of materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: LAW VII: The impression of the architecture is not to be dependent on size
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of parts of the building depend on delicacy of design, perfection of colour, preciousness of material, and legendary interest — qualities independent of size; thus the best work is concentrated within comparatively small spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect vast mass or soaring height; prefer low walls and touchable capitals where subtle sculpture and color can be appreciated. Avoid attempting to create architectural effect primarily by scale; evaluate success by delicacy and chromatic subtlety rather than magnitude.
